title: The Harvest of the Bell House
premise: Late-night radio host Noor Coldharbour begins receiving calls from listeners he buried grief for last week—each voice asking him to 'let them finish their sentence.' When the excavation crew beneath the old Bell House unearths a door sealed from the inside, the voices grow insistent: they were the ones who sealed it, and they need Noor's voice to keep it closed. Noor learns the station's frequency was never broadcasting outward but holding something in, and that his predecessors all paid with their identities to keep the door shut. At dawn, Noor chooses to surrender his own name to the door—becoming the next voice on the frequency—while his producer broadcasts the truth, freeing the town but erasing Noor from every memory but the tapes.
about_author: Ines Voss is the pen name of a former night-shift radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining transmitter towers in coastal fog belts. She writes horror about machines that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Living Callers
chapters.summary: POV Noor. During his 2 a.m. show, Noor takes a call from Marta Ellery—buried six days ago—and documents it obsessively, half-convinced he's cracking. More dead listeners call, each mid-sentence, each cut off by a sound like a door breathing. Emotional beat: dread wrapped in professional denial; Noor clings to documentation as sanity.

chapters.title: The Door Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: POV alternating Noor and excavation foreman Denny Kask. The crew breaks ground under the derelict Bell House and finds an iron door, bolted from the inside, warm to the touch. That night the callers stop asking to finish sentences and start asking Noor to 'keep talking, keep it asleep.' Emotional beat: the shift from mystery to complicity—Noor realizes his show has always been the lock.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: POV Noor. In the station's sealed archive, Noor finds decades of tapes: every host before him made the same bargain, feeding their names and memories into the frequency to hold the door. The thing inside offers Noor survival—walk away, forget, live—if someone else's voice replaces his. His producer, Rhee, volunteers. Emotional beat: temptation and guilt; power corrupting through the offer of escape at another's cost.

chapters.title: Sunrise Frequency
chapters.summary: POV Noor, then Rhee. As the door splits, Noor locks himself in the booth and gives the frequency his name, voice, and memory, holding it shut until dawn while Rhee broadcasts the archive to the town, breaking the cycle of secrecy. Noor survives only as the tapes. Emotional beat: sacrificial resolution—the price of survival finally paid in full, and paid willingly.
